catalog_quote: As all the words in the language are monosyllables, they are usually grouped together in groups of regular form and regular accentuation. These groups, of two, three, or four words (and sometimes of more), are often so absolutely fixed in the usage of the language as to become very similar to the polysyllabic words of other languages; and within such groups the laws of accent in relation to the several words are quite as strict as the accentual laws for the several syllables of the words in polysyllabic languages. The general rule is that the primary accent falls on the last word of a group, whether it be a group of two, three, or more words. When the accent falls on the second last or penult, I have indicated the fact by placing a double hyphen after the accented word. This has also the effect ... of indicating that the word which follows the double hyphen is enclitic. When two words making a group have no hyphen between them, the meaning is that the first word has a sort of secondary accent, and retains its own tone unchanged or but slightly changed; e.g. hong chhe, the wind blows; but in hong-chhe, a paper-kite, the "hong" is quite unaccented, as is shown by the presence of the hyphen. ... In a group of three words the general rule is that the primary accent falls on the last word, a secondary accent on the first, and that the second word is quite unaccented
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Min Nan (minn1241) is not in the catalog. Two title-works with stress in the title. (1) Hsu & Jun 1998 (UCLA WPP 96: 69-89) was obtained as the whole-issue scan from eScholarship (13.3 MB, no text; pp. 69-89 scanned at 300 dpi one page at a time) and read: it is a domain-initial strengthening study (EPG contact, closure duration, VOT, nasal airflow of Taiwanese stops at IP-/Word-/Syllable-initial position) and says nothing about where word stress falls -- prosody-but-not-word-stress, no-catalog-record. (2) Chiang 1994 (Delaware PhD, prosodic morphology of affixation in Taiwanese) could not be obtained or even abstracted from any open source; relevance to word stress unclear, priority low (it is a reduplication/affixation study per its only found citer, Rawski et al. 2023 Glossa). No first-hand stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title (nothing found); the earlier general check of this directory (05:13Z) already holds Duanmu 1990 and Chappell 2011/2019 as the stress-bearing sources for Min Nan.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Syllables (monosyllabic words) are organised into tone/accent groups of two to four; the primary accent falls on the group-final syllable, which alone keeps its full citation tone, while preceding syllables take changed (sandhi) tones; enclitic syllables (particles, pronouns, certain verbs/complements after the double hyphen) are unaccented and toneless, in which case the accent stands on the last non-enclitic syllable (penult or antepenult).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In a group of three, secondary accent normally on the first syllable with the middle one unaccented; secondary shifts to the second syllable when the first is an auxiliary/function word (u, bo, beh, prepositions, chit 'one', tsap 'ten') or the second has a 'stronger' tone; a group of four = two groups of two, each accented on its second syllable, the first sub-group weaker; faint secondary accent possible on the last of two enclitics.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (marked by double hyphen) are unaccented and lose their tone, so primary accent may fall on the penult or antepenult of the group; two-word groups written without hyphen (e.g. subject + verb hong chhe 'the wind blows') have secondary accent on the first word which keeps its tone; important content words may retain secondary accent against the tonal-strength tendency.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the accentual/tone group (2-4+ syllables, often lexicalised 'like polysyllabic words'), i.e. the tone-sandhi group rather than the morphological word; statement concerns connected speech and citation of fixed groups in Amoy (Xiamen) Hokkien. Language is tonal (7 tones); accent interacts with tone sandhi (only the accented final syllable keeps citation tone). Modern sources agree: Chen 1987 apud Duanmu 1990 (main stress on last non-weak syllable of the tone group), Chappell 2019, Ang 1998 (final rime 2.2x longer), Peng & Beckman 2003 (grouping-based prosody).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Douglas 1873) describes the Amoy (Xiamen) vernacular with Zhangzhou/Quanzhou variants, i.e. Hokkien/Quanzhang (Glottolog xiam1236 Xiamen, under hokk1242 Quanzhang, under minn1241). Corroborating modern sources cover Taiwanese Southern Min (taib1242 etc; Ang 1998, Peng & Beckman 2003, Chappell 2019) and Zhangzhou (fuji1236; Huang 2018). Chaoshan/Teochew (chao1238) and other Min Nan branches are not covered by the statement.

tone_statements.quote: There are seven lexical tones in Taiwan Min, including five unchecked tones that occur in CV(N) syllables – high-level /55/, low-rising /13/, high-falling /51/, low-falling /31/, and mid-level /33/ – and two checked tones that occur in CV [p t k ʔ] syllables – high-checked /5/ and low-checked /3/ (Figure 1). ... tone_statements.translation: Taiwanese has seven tones. [chart: yin-ping, yin-shang, yin-qu, yin-ru, yang-ping, yang-shang, yang-qu, yang-ru / tones 1-8] ... From the traditional yin/yang dualism this sound system has been said to have the four tones ping-shang-qu-ru in both the yin and the yang series, i.e. eight tones. But the results of physical experiments, as in the chart above, show that yin-shang (tone 2) and yang-shang (tone 6) are completely identical in shape, so in fact one should say there are seven. ... Yin-ping (tone 1): high and level, sustained rather long. ... Yang-ping (tone 5) ... the only rising tone, highly characteristic. ... Besides these there is the neutral tone (qingsheng).

tone_statements.citation: Li, Yen-hui Audrey & Wei, Wei Haley. 2019. Microparameters and language variation. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 4(1): 106. doi:10.5334/gjgl.938
tone_statements.quote: In TSM, every phrase or sentence consists of tone groups. Tone grouping dictates whether or not tones undergo changes. A changed tone takes the value of another lexical tone. The tone change rule in TSM is that every syllable in a phrase takes the combination tone, except the final syllable. The last syllable of a phrase has the isolation tone. Both combination and isolation tones are full lexical tones. [...] The important generalization is that every syllable within a tone group is pronounced with a regular lexical tone. There is no weakening of a syllable within a tone group.

sources.note: Instrumental: Taiwanese has no lexical neutral tone in compounds; all compound syllables are 'stressed' (重讀) but the compound-final rime is 2.22x longer than the non-final (308.8 vs 139.4 ms); affixes (阿-, -仔) and enclitic suffixes are unstressed (short) whether or not toneless; argues duration is the main correlate of stress and distinguishes 'unstressed' from 'neutral tone'.

sources.citation: Hsu, Chai-Shune K. & Sun-Ah Jun. 1998. Prosodic strengthening in Taiwanese: Syntagmatic or paradigmatic? UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 96: 69-89.
sources.quote: In this paper, we will examine first whether Taiwanese shows domain-initial strengthening. That is, whether the stop gesture is strengthened in domain-initial positions by enhancing laryngeal features or any other underlying features of the segment. For this, we have chosen three prosodic units: Intonational Phrase (IP), Word (Wd) and Syllable (S). Ideally, we should have a small-phrase level between IP and Wd as shown in Figure 1, but our only candidate, Tone Sandhi Group, was not considered since it has been argued in Chen (1987) that the Tone Sandhi Group is not strictly layered under IP, and Hayes (1990) also argued that Tone Sandhi Group is not a prosodic unit (p. 73)
sources.note: Nothing on word-stress placement. The paper is an EPG / closure-duration / VOT / nasal-airflow study of Taiwanese stops (/k^h/, /t/, /b/) at IP-initial vs Word-initial vs Syllable-initial position, three Tainan speakers; conclusion (p. 85): 'Taiwanese exhibits prosodic strengthening at prosodic domain-initial positions.. realized as paradigmatic contrast enhancement'. The only mentions of stress are generic (English/Italian/Korean prominence literature in Table 1). It is silent on whether Taiwanese words have stress and where it falls; it treats prosodic structure in terms of phrase edges, no…

sources.quote: There are seven lexical tones in Taiwan Min, including five unchecked tones that occur in CV(N) syllables – high-level /55/, low-rising /13/, high-falling /51/, low-falling /31/, and mid-level /33/ – and two checked tones that occur in CV [p t k ʔ] syllables – high-checked /5/ and low-checked /3/ (Figure 1). ... The six sandhi rules in Taiwan Min form two chain relationships: 13 → 33 → 31 → 51 → 55 and 3 → 5 → 3 (Cheng 1968, 1973). These six sandhi rules yield six sandhi tones and seven juncture tones (Figure 1).

tone.translation: Taiwanese has seven tones. [chart: yin-ping, yin-shang, yin-qu, yin-ru, yang-ping, yang-shang, yang-qu, yang-ru / tones 1-8] ... From the traditional yin/yang dualism this sound system has been said to have the four tones ping-shang-qu-ru in both the yin and the yang series, i.e. eight tones. But the results of physical experiments, as in the chart above, show that yin-shang (tone 2) and yang-shang (tone 6) are completely identical in shape, so in fact one should say there are seven. ... Yin-ping (tone 1): high and level, sustained rather long. ... Yang-ping (tone 5) ... the only rising tone, highly characteristic. ... Besides these there is the neutral tone (qingsheng).
